annotation: Treated the surviving spouse as a qualifying surviving spouse even though no dependent child is listed, which is required for that status. It therefore applied the $32,000/$44,000 joint Social Security thresholds (taxable SS $11,542 instead of $18,542.70) and a joint $32,300 standard deduction. Single status gives deductions of $18,150 + $6,000 and taxable income of $26,287.11.

AGI of $50,436 was correct, but it used the qualifying-surviving-spouse $32,200 joint standard deduction and a $1,650 aged add-on even though there is no dependent. Single status gives $16,100 + $2,050, plus the $6,000 senior deduction, which makes taxable income $26,287.11 instead of $10,586. That income is taxed at 10%/12%.

Wrongly counted the $48,000 of nontaxable veterans benefits in income and subtracted ESI premiums from AGI despite having no wages. It also taxed the full 85% of Social Security. After its own math produced about $6,600 of tax, it switched to $0 for no stated reason. The correct path is AGI $50,437.11 minus $24,150 of deductions, which gives tax of $2,906.45.

Claimed taxable income was zero without computing it. AGI is $50,437.11 ($24,000 pension + $7,849 IRA + $45 interest + $18,542.70 taxable SS), and the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction leave $26,287.11 taxable. That produces $2,906.45 of tax.

Filing status and deductions ($18,150 + $6,000) were right, but the second-tier Social Security formula used half of benefits ($13,048) instead of the $4,500 cap. That made taxable SS $22,182 instead of $18,542.70 and AGI $54,076 instead of $50,437.11. It also ended the 10% bracket at $12,150 instead of $12,400.

Applied qualifying-surviving-spouse joint status and a joint standard deduction of about $32,300 even though no dependent child is listed. It also taxed the full 85% of Social Security, then cut its own positive taxable-income estimate to $0 with no supporting calculation. Under Single status, taxable income is $26,287.11 and tax is $2,906.45.

Correctly used Single status and $24,150 of deductions, but taxed the full 85% cap of Social Security ($22,182) instead of $18,542.70. That overstated AGI by about $3,640. It then cut its own roughly $3,300 tax figure to an arbitrary $1,176 instead of applying 10%/12% to $26,287.11.

Computed AGI correctly but deducted the joint/QSS standard deduction ($32,200 + $1,650) even though a surviving spouse without a dependent files Single. Single gives $16,100 + $2,050 + $6,000 = $24,150, leaving $26,287.11 taxable, with part of it in the 12% bracket.

Used qualifying-surviving-spouse joint status (about $31,550 standard deduction and joint brackets) without a qualifying child. It taxed the full 85% of Social Security ($22,182 instead of $18,542.70) and left out the $6,000 senior deduction.

Applied the joint/QSS $33,850 standard deduction and brackets despite there being no dependent, taxed the full 85% of Social Security, and left out the $6,000 senior deduction. It then raised its own $2,023 figure to an unsupported $3,204.

Used the single Social Security thresholds and the correct $50,436 AGI, but deducted the joint/QSS standard deduction ($32,200 + $1,650) instead of the Single $16,100 + $2,050. That understated taxable income at $10,586 instead of $26,287.11.

AGI was correct, but it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction for filers 65 and older. It also understated the 2026 single standard deduction ($15,400 instead of $16,100), so taxable income came out at $32,986 instead of $26,287.11.

Taxed the full 85% of Social Security ($22,182) instead of the $18,542.70 the tiered formula produces, used a $17,350 standard deduction instead of $18,150, and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. Taxable income came out at $36,726 instead of $26,287.11.

Assumed TCJA expired in 2026, so it applied a $5,300 personal exemption and a 15% bracket. In fact, the OBBBA made the $16,100 + $2,050 standard deduction and the 12% bracket permanent and added the $6,000 senior deduction. It also itemized the employer-sponsored insurance premiums as a medical expense, which the engine's itemized total ($17,587.20 of SALT) does not include.

AGI and the $18,150 single age-65 standard deduction were correct, but it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. It also used a $12,200 top for the 10% bracket instead of $12,400. Taxable income was $32,286 instead of $26,287.11.

Assumed the 2026 TCJA sunset, so it used a $5,300 personal exemption and the 15% bracket and itemized ESI premiums as medical expenses. The OBBBA made the TCJA rules permanent, so the correct path is the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction, with 10%/12% brackets applied to $26,287.11.

Its stated taxable income of $37,990 omits the $6,000 senior deduction and is about $11,700 too high. Its $1,109 tax is not consistent with that income under any bracket schedule. The correct path is AGI $50,437.11 minus $24,150, giving $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

AGI was correct, but it applied pre-TCJA 2026 rules: a roughly $5,400 personal exemption, itemized real estate taxes, and a 15% bracket. The OBBBA kept the TCJA structure, so the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction apply, with no exemption and a 12% second bracket.

Assumed TCJA reverted in 2026, so it used a $5,050 personal exemption, itemized $16,470, and applied a 15% bracket. The applicable law has no personal exemption, an $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction, and a 12% second bracket.

Claimed income was below the deductions without computing either. AGI is $50,437.11 including $18,542.70 of taxable Social Security, and total deductions are only $24,150, which leaves $26,287.11 taxable.

Used the TCJA-sunset framework: itemized real estate taxes plus a personal exemption, taxed at 10%/15%. 2026 law has no personal exemption, an $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction, and 10%/12% brackets.

Assumed TCJA expired, so it took a personal exemption with itemized real estate taxes and the 15% bracket. The OBBBA kept the $16,100 + $2,050 standard deduction, added the $6,000 senior deduction, and kept the 12% bracket.
AGI was correct, but it used a $17,000 single age-65 standard deduction instead of $18,150 and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. Taxable income came out at $33,436 instead of $26,287.11.

Applied post-TCJA-expiration rules: a $5,300 personal exemption, a 15% bracket, and a medical deduction from ESI premiums. It also miscomputed taxable Social Security as $19,942 instead of $18,542.70. The correct path is the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction under the 10%/12% brackets.

Single status and AGI were correct, but it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. It also underestimated the standard deduction ($17,510 instead of $18,150) and the 10% bracket top ($12,283 instead of $12,400).

Itemized $21,076 by counting the $8,389 employer-sponsored insurance premiums as a medical deduction. The engine's itemized total is only $17,587.20 of SALT, so the $18,150 standard deduction applies. It also omitted the $6,000 senior deduction, which applies either way.

Used a surviving-spouse (joint) rate structure without a qualifying dependent and asserted the deductions wiped out all income. Under Single status, AGI of $50,437.11 minus $24,150 of deductions leaves $26,287.11 taxable.
Asserted that the standard deduction offsets all income without computing taxable Social Security. Taxable SS is $18,542.70, which puts AGI at $50,437.11, well above the $24,150 of total deductions.

Used surviving-spouse joint Social Security thresholds and the joint $32,200 standard deduction even though there is no dependent, which makes the filer Single. As a result, taxable SS came out at $11,542 instead of $18,542.70 and the deduction was overstated by about $14,000.

The method was right (Single status, $18,150 + $6,000 deductions, 10%/12% brackets), but taxable Social Security was overstated at $18,592 instead of $18,542.70. That inflated taxable income to $26,336 instead of $26,287.11.
Applied surviving-spouse joint thresholds and standard deduction without a qualifying dependent. That shrank taxable income to about $3,590 instead of the Single-status $26,287.11.
AGI was correct, but it applied the joint/QSS $33,850 age-adjusted standard deduction instead of the Single $18,150. Taxable income came out at $10,586 instead of $26,287.11.
Correct framework, but taxable Social Security was overstated by about $49, which put taxable income at $26,336 instead of $26,287.11. It also rounded the result to whole dollars.
Applied surviving-spouse joint Social Security thresholds (taxable SS $11,542) and the $33,850 joint standard deduction even though there is no dependent. The filer is Single.

Asserted without computation that senior deductions exceed taxable income, and wrongly listed nontaxable veterans benefits among the income items. Taxable SS is $18,542.70 and AGI is $50,437.11, so $26,287.11 remains after the $24,150 of deductions.
Applied pre-TCJA 2026 rules (a $5,300 personal exemption and a 15% bracket) and used the joint $23,200 10% bracket for a filer who is Single. It also omitted the $6,000 senior deduction.

Assumed the TCJA sunset, so it itemized property tax, added a personal exemption, and used 10%/15% brackets. The correct path is the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction, with the 10%/12% brackets applied to $26,287.11.
Deductions and taxable income were correct, but it ended the 2026 single 10% bracket at $12,200 instead of $12,400. That moved $200 into the 12% rate and produced $2,910 instead of $2,906.45.

Assumed the TCJA sunset (no SALT cap and a 15% bracket) and itemized ESI premiums as medical expenses, which the engine's $17,587.20 itemized total excludes. It also omitted the $6,000 senior deduction.

Gave no answer or reasoning for this output. The correct derivation gives AGI of $50,437.11, minus the $18,150 standard deduction and the $6,000 senior deduction, which taxed at 10%/12% yields $2,906.45.

Subtracted an inapplicable lifetime learning credit and a $750 elderly credit from its tax estimate. The elderly credit is zero because about $7,553 of nontaxable Social Security exceeds the $5,000 initial amount. No nonrefundable credits apply, so the tax on $26,287.11 stays at $2,906.45.
AGI, the $18,150 standard deduction, and the brackets were correct, but it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction for filers 65 and older. Taxable income came out at $32,286 instead of $26,287.11.

Left half of Social Security benefits out of provisional income (used $37,472 instead of $50,520) and dropped the $4,500 base amount. That made taxable Social Security $2,951.20 instead of $18,542.70, which understated AGI.

Used qualifying-widow joint status without a dependent and treated Social Security as fully nontaxable, even though provisional income of $50,520 exceeds the $34,000 threshold. The correct path is Single status with $18,542.70 of taxable SS.
Claimed the single age-65 standard deduction eliminates taxable income. AGI is $50,437.11, so even after the $18,150 standard deduction and the $6,000 senior deduction, $26,287.11 remains taxable.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The model treated age 77 and an asserted income exclusion calculation as sufficient for Texas aged Medicaid without identifying or satisfying an aged eligibility pathway. The person qualifies through no Medicaid category and receives no SSI, so the claimed below-threshold aged eligibility does not apply.

The model correctly stated that no earned wages were reported and that payroll tax therefore equals zero, but then submitted $1,534 instead. Its numeric output contradicts its own payroll-tax-base analysis and the required final-value contract.
The model returned no payroll_tax value or explanation, so the required output was missing.

It computed AGI of $31,402.25 correctly but assumed the TCJA had sunset. So it used a $16,600 joint standard deduction plus $3,300 in aged additions, and added $10,600 in personal exemptions. That left $902.25 of taxable income. Under the permanent TCJA structure from P.L. 119-21, exemptions are $0 and the 2026 joint standard deduction is $32,200, which by itself exceeds AGI, so taxable income and tax are $0.

It explicitly assumed the TCJA sunset in 2026. It deducted a projected $15,150 standard deduction, $3,100 in aged additions and $10,100 in personal exemptions, totaling $28,350, which left $3,052.25 taxed at 10%. P.L. 119-21 kept personal exemptions at $0 and set the 2026 joint standard deduction at $32,200, which is above the $31,402.25 AGI, so tax is $0.

It applied pre-TCJA-style deductions for 2026: a $19,600 standard deduction including the aged additions, plus $10,000 in personal exemptions. That left $1,802.25 of taxable income. Personal exemptions remain $0 permanently under P.L. 119-21, and the 2026 joint standard deduction of $32,200 alone wipes out the $31,402.25 AGI, before the aged addition and the $6,000-per-senior deduction.

It reasoned 'after TCJA expiration' and deducted a $16,600 standard deduction, a $3,200 aged addition and $10,600 in personal exemptions, totaling $30,400. That left $1,002.25 taxed at 10%. The TCJA did not expire: P.L. 119-21 made the $0 exemption and the higher standard deduction permanent. The 2026 joint standard deduction is $32,200, which exceeds the $31,402.25 AGI, so tax is $0.

It counted $11,588 of Social Security as taxable by using the 85% formula, even though combined income of $36,677 is below the $44,000 joint second threshold. Only the 50% tier applies, so taxable Social Security is $2,338.25 and AGI is $31,402.25, not $40,652. It then used a sunset-era $20,400 deduction built from a $12,700 base, although its stated components sum to only $16,070. The actual 2026 joint standard deduction under P.L. 119-21 is $32,200, which exceeds the correct AGI and gives $0 tax.

The model named the correct SSI-related aged pathway but asserted rather than computed the SSI income test: applying the $20 general exclusion, the $65 earned-income exclusion, and the one-half earned-income disregard gives countable income of about $15,205 from Social Security plus about $14,500 from wages, roughly $2,475 per month, far above the couple SSI federal benefit rate and above Virginia's ~80% FPL aged/blind/disabled limit, which is why SSI received is 0 and medicaid_category is NONE. It compounded this by treating Medicare Savings Program status (QMB/SLMB) and medically needy spend-down as Medicaid-eligibility categories, neither of which is a qualifying pathway here, and by never noticing that household income at 2.05x FPL exceeds even the 100% FPL QMB test.

The model invented a rule that PolicyEngine's aged category is age-only with no income test; the aged/disabled pathway is SSI-linked and requires passing both the SSI income and asset tests, which this household fails with $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security. Because SSI is 0, no category attaches and medicaid_category resolves to NONE despite the head being 71.

The model supplied no rule at all and defaulted age 71 to Medicaid eligibility. Age 71 removes the head from the MAGI expansion adult group (which ends at 64) and routes eligibility to the SSI-linked aged pathway, whose income and asset tests this household fails, so the correct derivation yields no qualifying category; the model's answer is consistent with an age-alone heuristic that skips every income test.

The model equated Medicare Savings Program status with Medicaid eligibility, concluding the head qualifies "as a Medicare savings program recipient"; MSP buy-in is not a PolicyEngine Medicaid eligibility category, and the head qualifies through none of the actual pathways. It also mischaracterized $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security as low income when that is 2.05x FPL, above both the MAGI thresholds and the 100% FPL QMB limit it implicitly relied on.
The model correctly computed Social Security tax of $1,801.968 and Medicare tax of $421.428 but failed to add them correctly. Their sum rounds to $2,223.39, not $4,412.33.

The model understated employee FICA by failing to apply the combined 7.65% Social Security and Medicare rate accurately to all $29,064 of wages. The two components are $1,801.97 and $421.43, totaling $2,223.39 rather than $2,090.

The model used the correct 7.65% FICA rate but rounded the resulting liability to $2,220 instead of calculating and reporting the required dollar amount. Applying 7.65% to $29,064 yields $2,223.396 before component-level cent rounding and $2,223.39 from the separately rounded Social Security and Medicare components.

The model incorrectly treated reaching full retirement age as an exemption from employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. Wages remain subject to FICA regardless of retirement age, producing $1,801.97 of Social Security tax and $421.43 of Medicare tax.

The model incorrectly bypassed the gross-income eligibility limit because both household members are elderly and proceeded directly to a speculative net-income calculation. It also treated the mortgage balance as though it established deductible shelter expenses, even though no rent, mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, or utility expense was listed; the $44,289 gross income instead fails the threshold and yields value = 0.

The model correctly computed that the $44,289 household MAGI exceeds 138% FPL for a couple, then overrode its own finding by asserting an aged pathway that tests the spouse's individual income ('spouse with no own income may qualify'). The SSI-related aged/blind/disabled test counts the couple's combined countable income under spousal deeming, not the spouse's zero personal earnings, and Virginia's ABD standard of roughly 80% FPL (about $17,300 for two) is failed by $44,289 by a factor of 2.5; with $0 SSI received, the SSI-recipient route is closed as well.

The model identified the correct pathway, Virginia's aged/blind/disabled category, but misstated its income limit, claiming $15,225 of Social Security plus $29,064 of wages sits 'well under the ABD income and resource limits for a couple after standard disregards.' Virginia's ABD categorically needy standard is about 80% FPL (roughly $17,300 annually for a couple), and the SSI disregards ($20 general, $65 plus half the remainder on earnings) still leave about $29,100 of countable annual income, so the couple fails the income test by more than $10,000; the resource check the model relied on is irrelevant once income disqualifies.

The model invented a rule, asserting that PolicyEngine places everyone 65+ in an 'aged eligibility category, which carries no income test.' No Medicaid category is conferred by age alone: the 65+ non-MAGI route requires SSI receipt or countable income within the state's SSI-related ABD standard (about 80% FPL) plus the $3,000 couple resource limit, and with $0 SSI and $44,289 of household income the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE.

The model applied no eligibility test at all, defaulting a 69-year-old to 'potentially eligible' on age alone. Running the actual tests yields ineligibility on both branches: age 69 falls outside the 19-64 expansion adult group and the MAGI of 2.05x FPL exceeds the 138% FPL ceiling, while the non-MAGI aged route fails because SSI received is $0 and $44,289 of couple income is far above Virginia's roughly 80% FPL ABD standard.

The model conflated the Medicare Savings Programs with Medicaid eligibility, reasoning that the spouse 'qualifies for Medicaid as Medicare savings program recipient in Virginia.' MSP premium assistance is not a Medicaid eligibility category here, and the household fails it regardless: the QMB limit is 100% FPL while this couple sits at 2.05x FPL. The model also called the 69-year-old 'eligible for Medicare soon' when Medicare eligibility attached at 65, and it never applied any income test to the actual aged/blind/disabled pathway.

The model incorrectly treated 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment as a prerequisite for Medicare eligibility rather than a condition for premium-free Part A. Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.

Substituted "two $1,000 aged exemptions" for Virginia's $12,000-per-person age deduction under Va. Code § 58.1-322.02(10)-(11); the additional 65+ exemption is $800 and sits on top of that age deduction, which is unreduced here because AFYA of $29,064 is far below the $75,000 joint phase-out. Two full $12,000 age deductions exceed the $29,064 of Virginia AGI on their own, so taxable income is $0 rather than the $9,164 it computed. It also ran the 2% bracket to $5,000 when Virginia's 2% bracket stops at $3,000.

Carried federal AGI of $31,402.25 straight into Virginia without the § 58.1-322.02(4) subtraction for the $2,338.25 of federally taxable Social Security, so its Virginia AGI is $2,338 too high. It then allowed only $21,484 of total deductions — less than the $24,000 of age deductions alone, since both spouses are 65+ and AFYA of $29,064 sits below the $75,000 joint threshold. Correct Virginia AGI of $29,064 less $24,000 of age deductions plus the standard deduction and exemptions leaves $0 taxable income and $0 tax.

Gave no derivation, and its $560 corresponds to roughly $13,800 of Virginia taxable income ($60 + $60 + 5% of $8,800) — that is $29,064 of Virginia AGI reduced only by a standard deduction and personal exemptions, with no age deduction at all. Virginia's $12,000 age deduction applies to each spouse here because both are 65+ and AFYA of $29,064 is below the $75,000 joint reduction threshold, so $24,000 alone drives taxable income to $0.

Took the Virginia Social Security subtraction correctly but invented an offset in which the head's $12,000 age deduction is consumed by the $15,225 of Social Security benefits received; Virginia reduces the age deduction only for adjusted federal AGI over $75,000 on a joint return, and that measure excludes taxable Social Security entirely, so each spouse keeps the full $12,000. It also applied the $8,500 single standard deduction to a joint return. With $24,000 of age deductions against $29,064 of Virginia AGI, taxable income is $0, not $6,704.

Its $250.20 implies about $7,600 of Virginia taxable income, i.e. roughly $21,460 of total deductions against $29,064 of Virginia AGI — consistent with a single $12,000 age deduction plus the standard deduction and exemptions, not the "two age deductions" its explanation claims. Both spouses are 65 or older and combined AFYA of $29,064 is below the $75,000 joint phase-out, so $24,000 of age deductions applies and by itself exceeds Virginia AGI, leaving $0 of taxable income and $0 of tax.

Treated Virginia's age benefit as the $1,600 of "age/blind additions" — the two $800 additional 65+ exemptions — and never claimed the separate $12,000-per-person age deduction of § 58.1-322.02(10)-(11), which is unreduced because AFYA of $29,064 is far under the $75,000 joint threshold. Adding the missing $24,000 to its own $16,000 standard deduction and $1,860 of exemptions eliminates the $9,600 of taxable income it computed, so the tax is $0 rather than $350.

Put the entire $15,225 of Social Security into federal AGI for a $44,289 starting point when only $2,338.25 is federally taxable under the 50% tier, and then never applied Virginia's subtraction for that taxable portion — Virginia AGI is $29,064. It also discarded its own branch that used the correct $24,000 of age deductions and submitted $739.15, a figure none of its three calculations ($449.37, $33.78, and the $10,989 taxable-income branch) produces. Virginia AGI of $29,064 less $24,000 of age deductions plus the standard deduction and exemptions yields $0 taxable income and $0 tax.

In its final recalculation the model added the $24,000 disability benefits back into income ($42,740 other income). It applied the single-filer Social Security thresholds of $25,000/$34,000 instead of the MFJ $32,000/$44,000, and used a single $20,550 deduction and single brackets instead of the joint $35,500 deduction plus $12,000 senior deduction. With disability excluded and MFJ rules applied, AGI is $23,130, which is less than the deductions, so tax is $0.

The model counted the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable, which raised other income and pushed taxable Social Security to $23,663 instead of $4,390. It also used a $15,650 single-style deduction plus personal exemptions, which are suspended, and a 15% bracket that no longer exists. It never applied the MFJ 65+ deduction of $35,500 plus the $12,000 senior deduction, which would bring the correct $23,130 AGI to $0 tax.

The model's reasoning concludes that the MFJ 65+ standard deduction exceeds AGI and ends with 'value = 0', but the submitted numeric value is $120.30. That number contradicts its own explanation, so the error is in the output, not the tax analysis.

The model treated the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable, which produced an AGI of $66,403 with $23,663 of taxable Social Security. The correct AGI is $23,130 with only $4,390 of Social Security taxable. It also used personal exemptions, which are suspended, and a 15% bracket instead of the $35,500 MFJ 65+ deduction plus the $12,000 senior deduction.

The model correctly left out the disability benefits but counted the full $44,080 of Social Security as taxable instead of running the provisional-income test. That test gives provisional income of $40,780, which is under $44,000, so only 50% × ($40,780 − $32,000) = $4,390 is taxable. It also left out the $12,000 senior deduction. The correct AGI of $23,130 is below the deductions, so tax is $0.

The model included the $24,000 disability benefits in taxable income, which inflated the Social Security inclusion and gave a positive taxable income of about $22,203. PolicyEngine excludes disability benefits from gross income, so AGI is only $23,130, the joint standard, age, and senior deductions reduce taxable income to zero, and tax is $0.

The model counted 'disability income' as taxable alongside the pension, interest, and Social Security, which gave a large positive taxable income. With the $24,000 disability benefits excluded, taxable Social Security is $4,390 and AGI is $23,130, below the $35,500 MFJ 65+ standard deduction alone, so tax is $0.

The model included the $24,000 disability benefits in provisional income, and then treated the full 85% cap ($37,468) as taxable Social Security. Even under its own figures, the formula gives min($37,468, 85% × ($64,780 − $44,000) + $6,000 = $23,663). It also left out the $12,000 senior deduction. With disability excluded, taxable Social Security is $4,390, AGI is $23,130, and tax is $0.

The model treated the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable, which gave an AGI of $66,403 instead of $23,130. It also deducted only $35,500 and left out the $12,000 senior deduction ($6,000 per spouse 65+). Without the disability benefits, AGI is below the standard deduction and tax is $0.

The model applied the deductions correctly, totaling $47,500, but counted the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable. That raised AGI to $66,403 and taxable Social Security to $23,663. PolicyEngine excludes disability benefits, so AGI is $23,130 with only $4,390 of Social Security taxable, and taxable income and tax are both $0.

The model excluded the disability benefits in its final pass but declared the full $44,080 of Social Security taxable. Its own combined income of $40,780 falls below the $44,000 MFJ second threshold, so only 50% × ($40,780 − $32,000) = $4,390 is taxable. It also used a $32,600 deduction that leaves out the $12,000 senior deduction. The correct AGI of $23,130 gives $0 tax.

The model correctly identified a zero taxable wage base and then contradicted that computation by inventing taxable wage-equivalent income and assigning $1,926 of Social Security and Medicare taxes. No listed income is employee compensation subject to payroll tax, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax components all equal zero.

The model incorrectly evaluated the spouse as a separate zero-income individual and assumed that age alone opened an aged Medicaid pathway. Washington's pathway evaluation includes the applicable household income and categorical requirements; this spouse receives no SSI, has household MAGI of 2.90 times FPL, and qualifies for no category.

Its own reasoning reached about $22,379, close to the correct figure but using a $32,300 standard deduction instead of $32,200. It then submitted $27,049, which doesn't follow from that work. The submitted number matches a TCJA-sunset calculation (personal exemptions and 25% bracket), and 2026 law does not use those rules.

It subtracted $500 of auto-loan interest as a deduction on top of the $32,200 standard deduction. That $500 is ordinary household auto-loan interest, not qualified vehicle-loan interest, so it isn't deductible here. The correct taxable income is $151,090.25, not $150,590.50, and the extra deduction cut the tax by exactly 22% × $500 = $110.

It deducted the traditional 401(k) ($23,926) and IRA ($1,118) contributions even though there are no wages or other compensation to support them. It also figured taxable Social Security as 85% of the excess over $32,000 ($23,384) instead of the $50,583 cap. Finally, it used a $28,900 standard deduction with an over-65 addition, but neither spouse is 65 and the 2026 MFJ amount is $32,200.

It gave a rough $14,800 without working through the brackets and was unsure about 65+ status. Neither spouse is 65, so no additional or senior deduction applies. On $151,090.25 of taxable income, the 2026 MFJ brackets plus 15% on qualified dividends produce $22,400.65.

Its reasoning reached about $22,652 using 2025-level brackets (10% to $24,150, 12% to $98,200). It then submitted an unsupported $19,524, citing 'estimation uncertainty'. The correct 2026 brackets (10% to $24,800, 12% to $100,800) on $147,330.25 of ordinary income give $21,836.65, plus $564 on dividends.

It used 2025 bracket thresholds (10% to $23,850, 12% to $96,950) and a $32,300 standard deduction. The 2026 MFJ values are $24,800, $100,800, and $32,200. Because the lower thresholds push more income into the 22% bracket, it overstated tax by about $380.

It said it applied a 24% bracket to about $147,331 of ordinary income and got $23,886. The 24% bracket doesn't start until $211,400 for 2026 MFJ, so all of the income above $100,800 belongs at 22%. Correct ordinary tax is $21,836.65.
